questions.question: An infinite set $X$ is countably infinite exactly when:
options: there is a bijection between $X$ and $\mathbb{N}$
questions.explanation: An infinite set $X$ is countably infinite exactly when there is a bijection from $X$ to $\mathbb{N}$. Under the Math II convention, countable sets include both finite and countably infinite sets.
questions.source_support: A set is countably infinite if it has the same cardinality as $\mathbb{N}$.
questions.rewrite_notes: Aligned the definition with Math II by distinguishing countably infinite from the broader term countable.
option_explanations: Having more elements than R would make X larger than R, not countable.
Having no proper subsets is unrelated to countability.
Being a subset of N is sufficient but not necessary for countability.

questions.question: An infinite set is called uncountable when:
options: no bijection between it and $\mathbb{N}$ exists
it can be listed as a sequence
it is a subset of every finite set
questions.explanation: An infinite set is uncountable when no bijection between it and N exists.
questions.source_support: In the absence of a bijection with $\mathbb{N}$, an infinite set is uncountable.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: Having finitely many elements makes it finite, not uncountable.
Being listable as a sequence means it is countable, not uncountable.
Being a subset of every finite set is unrelated to uncountability.

questions.question: Which of these sets is countable?
options: the set of all intervals in $\mathbb{R}$
questions.explanation: Q (the rationals) is countable — it can be listed as a sequence indexed by N.
questions.source_support: $\mathbb{Q}$ is countable.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: R is uncountable (Cantor's diagonal argument).
R minus Q (the irrationals) is uncountable.
The set of all intervals in R is uncountable.

questions.question: Which of these sets is uncountable?
questions.explanation: R is uncountable (proved by Cantor's diagonal argument).
questions.source_support: $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable.
questions.rewrite_notes: Clarified that finite sets are countable under the Math II convention.
option_explanations: Q is countable.
N is countable.
$\{1,2,3\}$ is finite and therefore countable under the Math II convention, so it is not uncountable.

questions.question: According to the classification, an infinite set must be:
questions.explanation: An infinite set must be either countable or uncountable (the two categories are exhaustive for infinite sets).
questions.source_support: An infinite set is either countable or uncountable.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: Not all infinite sets are countable (R is a counterexample).
Not all infinite sets are uncountable (N is countable).
An infinite set cannot become finite by relabelling.

questions.question: What does it mean, intuitively, that a set is countably infinite?
options: Its elements can be listed in a sequence.
It has only finitely many elements.
Its elements cannot be compared with $\mathbb{N}$.
questions.explanation: A countably infinite set can be listed as a sequence indexed by $\mathbb{N}$ without omitting any element. The list has no final element because the set is infinite.
questions.source_support: A countably infinite set has a bijection with $\mathbb{N}$ and can therefore be listed as a sequence.
questions.rewrite_notes: Reworded the item to test countably infinite rather than incorrectly treating every countable set as infinite.
option_explanations: A countably infinite set is not finite; this option drops the infinite part of the definition.
A countable set is not larger than R (it is smaller).
A countable set can be compared with N via a bijection.

questions.question: Is $\mathbb{N}$ countable?
options: Yes, the identity map is a bijection $\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$
Only if $\mathbb{N}$ is treated as finite
questions.explanation: $\mathbb{N}$ is countably infinite because its identity map is a bijection from $\mathbb{N}$ to itself. Hence it is also countable under the Math II convention.
questions.source_support: $\mathbb{N}$ is countably infinite and therefore countable.
questions.rewrite_notes: Removed the obsolete claim that countable sets are infinite by definition.
option_explanations: Being infinite does not prevent countability; $\mathbb{N}$ is the standard countably infinite set.
Being a subset of R does not prevent countability.
N is infinite, not finite.

questions.question: What does the subset result say about a subset $A$ of a countable set?
questions.explanation: Every subset of a countable set is countable. The subset may be finite or countably infinite, and both cases fall under the Math II definition of countable.
questions.skill_detail: key result: subset of countable is finite or countable
questions.source_support: Every subset of a countable set is countable.
questions.rewrite_notes: Updated the subset result so finite subsets are included within countable rather than treated as a separate category.
option_explanations: A subset of a countable set cannot be uncountable.
A countable subset need not equal $\mathbb{N}$; for example, $\{1,2,3\}$ is a proper finite subset.
A countable subset may be finite, such as $\{1,2,3\}$, so it need not be infinite.

questions.question: If $A\subseteq\mathbb{Q}$ is infinite, what follows?
questions.explanation: If A is a subset of Q and A is infinite, then A is countable (subset of a countable set).
questions.skill_detail: apply subset result to A subset of Q
questions.source_support: Subsets of countable sets are finite or countable; $\mathbb{Q}$ is countable.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: A is countable, not uncountable.

$A\subseteq\mathbb{Q}$ but $\mathbb{R}\nsubseteq\mathbb{Q}$ (irrationals such as $\sqrt{2}$ are not rational), so $A$ cannot equal $\mathbb{R}$; the conclusion is that $A$ is countable, not a jump to $\mathbb{R}$.

An infinite subset of $\mathbb{Q}$ need not be all of $\mathbb{Q}$: $\mathbb{Z}\subseteq\mathbb{Q}$ is infinite and countable but $\mathbb{Z}\ne\mathbb{Q}$. The subset result only forces $A$ to be countable.

questions.question: Why is it wrong to say every infinite set is countable?
options: every infinite set is actually finite
questions.explanation: Not every infinite set is countable: R is infinite but uncountable.
questions.skill_detail: misconception: not every infinite set is countable
questions.source_support: $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable, showing infinite does not imply countable.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: Infinite sets are not finite.
N has a bijection with itself (the identity), so it is countable.
Q is countable, not uncountable.

questions.question: How do uncountable sets compare in size with countable sets?
options: They are strictly larger than countable sets
They have the same size as $\mathbb{N}$
They are exactly the subsets of $\mathbb{N}$
questions.explanation: Uncountable sets are strictly larger than countable sets (no bijection exists between them).
questions.source_support: Uncountable sets are strictly larger than countable ones.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: Uncountable sets are larger, not smaller.
Uncountable sets do not have the same size as N.
Uncountable sets are not subsets of N (they are too large).

questions.question: $\mathbb{Q}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$. Does that make $\mathbb{Q}$ uncountable?
options: No: $\mathbb{Q}$ is countable despite being dense
questions.explanation: Q is countable despite being dense in R; density does not imply uncountability.
questions.source_support: $\mathbb{Q}$ is countable.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: Density does not force uncountability (Q is a counterexample).
Filling the line does not imply uncountability.
It can be decided: Q is countable.

questions.question: To prove an infinite set $X$ is countable, what is enough?
questions.explanation: To prove X is countable, it suffices to exhibit one bijection between X and N.
questions.source_support: Countability requires the existence of a bijection with $\mathbb{N}$.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: One failed bijection does not prove uncountability.
Being infinite is necessary but not sufficient for countability.
Being a subset of R does not prove countability.

questions.question: Is $\mathbb{Z}$ countable?
questions.explanation: Z is countable: it is an infinite subset of the countable set Q.
questions.skill_detail: Z countable via subset of Q
questions.source_support: Subsets of countable sets are finite or countable; $\mathbb{Q}$ is countable.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: Including negative numbers does not prevent countability.
Being infinite does not prevent countability.
Z is infinite, not finite.

questions.question: Can a subset of an uncountable set be countable?
options: Yes: $\mathbb{N}\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ is countable while $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable
No, subsets of uncountable sets are always uncountable
No, because subsets are always smaller and hence finite
Only if the subset equals the whole set
questions.explanation: Yes, a subset of an uncountable set can be countable: N is a subset of R, N is countable, R is uncountable.
questions.skill_detail: counterexample: subset of uncountable can be countable
questions.source_support: $\mathbb{N}$ is countable and $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: Subsets of uncountable sets can be countable (N in R is an example).
Subsets can be smaller and still infinite (not necessarily finite).

$\mathbb{N}\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ is a proper subset ($\mathbb{N}\ne\mathbb{R}$) and is countable, so a countable subset of an uncountable set can be proper; equality with the whole uncountable set is not required.

questions.question: Under the Math II convention, what must be established to prove a set $X$ is uncountable?
options: $X$ is infinite and no bijection $X\to\mathbb{N}$ exists.
One attempted bijection $X\to\mathbb{N}$ happens to fail.
$X$ is infinite, without comparing it with $\mathbb{N}$.
No bijection $X\to\mathbb{N}$ exists, even if $X$ is finite.
questions.explanation: An uncountable set is one that is neither finite nor countably infinite. Thus $X$ must be infinite, and every possible bijection between $X$ and $\mathbb{N}$ must be ruled out.
questions.skill_detail: necessity: must show NO bijection exists
questions.source_support: A set is countable if it is finite or countably infinite; otherwise it is uncountable.
questions.rewrite_notes: Added the required infinitude condition because finite sets also lack a bijection with N but remain countable.
option_explanations: Failure of one proposed map rules out only that map; another bijection could still exist.
$\mathbb{N}$ itself is infinite but countably infinite, so infinitude alone does not imply uncountability.
A finite set also has no bijection with $\mathbb{N}$, but finite sets are countable under the course convention.

questions.question: If $A\subseteq X$ and $A$ is uncountable, what can you conclude about $X$?
questions.explanation: If A is a subset of X and A is uncountable, then X must be uncountable (a countable X cannot contain an uncountable subset).
questions.source_support: Subsets of countable sets are finite or countable, so an uncountable subset forces $X$ uncountable.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: X cannot be countable (it contains an uncountable subset).
X cannot be finite (it contains an uncountable subset).

$\mathbb{N}$ is countable, so it cannot contain an uncountable subset at all; $X$ must be uncountable, which $\mathbb{N}$ is not. For instance $X=\mathbb{R}$ with $A=(0,1)$ works, and $\mathbb{R}\ne\mathbb{N}$.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes a countable set from a countably infinite set?
options: A countable set may be finite; a countably infinite set is listable without end.
Every countable set is infinite and can be listed in sequence.
A finite set is uncountable because it has no bijection with $\mathbb{N}$.
A countably infinite listing eventually reaches a final element.
questions.explanation: Math II uses countable for both finite and countably infinite sets. A countably infinite set can be listed by $\mathbb{N}$, but that infinite list never reaches a last element.
questions.skill_detail: countable infinite is still infinite, not finishable
questions.source_support: Countable means finite or countably infinite; countably infinite means bijective with $\mathbb{N}$.
questions.rewrite_notes: Replaced the old finite-versus-countable framing with the Math II distinction between countable and countably infinite.
option_explanations: Finite sets are also countable, so countable does not by itself imply infinite.
Finite sets are countable under this convention even though they are not in bijection with $\mathbb{N}$.
A countably infinite enumeration has no last element; reaching one would make the set finite.

questions.question: How is a finite set classified under the countable/uncountable distinction?
options: Finite, so neither countable nor uncountable.
It is both countable and uncountable.
questions.explanation: Under the Math II convention, every finite set is countable. The term countably infinite is reserved for infinite sets that are in bijection with $\mathbb{N}$.
questions.skill_detail: boundary: a finite set under this definition
questions.source_support: A set is countable if it is finite or countably infinite.
questions.rewrite_notes: Corrected the obsolete answer: changed correct_index from 0 to 1 because finite sets are countable in Math II.
option_explanations: Finite sets are included in the countable category, so they are not outside the classification.
A finite set is not classified as uncountable.
Countable and uncountable are mutually exclusive; a finite set is countable only.

questions.question: Is the set $S=\{1/n : n\in\mathbb{N},\ n\ge 1\}$ countable?
questions.explanation: The map $n\mapsto 1/n$ for integers $n\ge 1$ lists every element of $S$ exactly once. Thus $S$ is countably infinite and therefore countable.
questions.skill_detail: apply listability to a concrete set
questions.source_support: A set in bijection with the positive natural numbers is countably infinite and hence countable.
questions.rewrite_notes: Made the index set exclude zero explicitly and aligned the conclusion with countably infinite terminology.
option_explanations: Being a subset of R does not prevent countability.
Being bounded does not prevent countability.
The set is infinite, not finite.
